english: have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)
formNote: Attach -ㄹ 수밖에 없다 to vowel-ending stems (가다 → 갈 수밖에 없다) and -을 수밖에 없다 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을 수밖에 없다); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (살다 → 살 수밖에 없다). 밖에 means 'except,' so literally 'there is nothing except doing it.' With adjectives it means 'can't help being ~' (비싸다 → 비쌀 수밖에 없다 = it's bound to be expensive). Past: -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없었어요.
usage: I have no choice but to wait
I had no choice but to put up with it
Of course it's expensive (it can't help but be)
I had no choice but to go
examples: 막차 끊겨서 택시 탈 수밖에 없었어요.
The last train was gone, so I had no choice but to take a taxi.
막차 끊기다 = miss the last train; common late-night reality
월급은 그대론데 물가는 오르니까 아낄 수밖에 없죠.
My salary's the same but prices keep rising, so of course I have to save.
물가 = cost of living; relatable money talk
사장님이 시키는데 야근할 수밖에 없잖아.
The boss tells me to, so I've got no choice but to work overtime.
야근 = overtime; -잖아 shares the obvious
mistakes: Don't write 밖에 separately as 밖에 없다 with a space inside 수밖에 — it's 수밖에 (one chunk), then 없다.
Using -는 수밖에: the form is the future modifier -(으)ㄹ + 수밖에 없다 (갈 수밖에 없다), not 가는 수밖에.

english: there's no way that / it can't possibly be that
formNote: Attach -ㄹ 리가 없다 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 올 리가 없다) and -을 리가 없다 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을 리가 없다). 리 means 'reason/likelihood,' so it literally says 'there is no reason it would be so.' For the past, use -았/었을 리가 없다 (갔을 리가 없다 = no way they went). The 가 is often dropped in speech: -(으)ㄹ 리 없어요.
usage: There's no way that's the case
There's no way they've arrived already
There's no way this is free
이다 → 일 리가 없다 (N + 일 리가 없다)
examples: 그 맛집이 오늘 한가할 리가 없어요. 웨이팅 엄청날걸요.
No way that famous spot is quiet today — the wait's probably huge.
맛집 = popular eatery; 웨이팅 = line/wait
걔가 나 좋아할 리가 없잖아. 김칫국 마시지 마.
There's no way he likes me. Don't get ahead of yourself.
김칫국 마시다 = assume too soon; dating slang
월세가 이 가격일 리가 없는데, 사기 아니에요?
There's no way the rent is this cheap — isn't it a scam?
월세 = monthly rent; 사기 = scam, housing wariness
mistakes: Don't confuse 리 (likelihood) with the verb-stem 리- ; this 리 always follows the modifier -(으)ㄹ.
For a past doubt you need -았/었을 리가 없다 (했을 리가 없다); the plain present 할 리가 없다 means 'no way he would (do it),' not 'no way he did it.'

english: it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)
formNote: 셈 means a 'count/reckoning,' so this frames a situation as 'effectively the same as.' Present verbs take -는 셈이다 (사는 → 사는 셈이다), past verbs take -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (끝난 → 끝난 셈이다), and adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (싼 → 싼 셈이다). It's used when reality isn't literally X but practically counts as X. Often paired with 거의 (almost) or 다 (all).
usage: It's basically like I got it for free
I'm basically working overtime every day
Just count it as having eaten cheap
examples: 할인까지 하면 거의 반값에 산 셈이에요.
With the discount, I basically bought it half price.
Doing the mental math on a deal
출퇴근에 두 시간이면 하루의 절반을 길에서 보내는 셈이죠.
Two hours commuting means you basically spend half your day on the road.
출퇴근 = commute; relatable city life
이번 달 회식이 다섯 번이면 거의 매주 모인 셈이네.
Five company dinners this month means we basically met every week.
회식 = team dinner; 거의 reinforces 셈
mistakes: Match the modifier to tense/type: past action 끝난 셈, ongoing 하는 셈, adjective 싼 셈 — don't say 끝나는 셈 for a finished thing.
It's not a literal claim; 다 한 셈이에요 means 'practically done,' not '100% done,' so don't use it when something is truly complete.

english: might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)
formNote: Attach -ㄹ지도 모르다 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 올지도 모르다) and -을지도 모르다 to consonant-ending stems (늦다 → 늦을지도 모르다). It literally means 'I don't even know whether ~,' i.e. there's a real chance. For the past, use -았/었을지도 몰라요 (갔을지도 몰라요 = might have gone). The 도 can be dropped for a slightly stronger guess: -(으)ㄹ지 몰라요.
usage: He might be busy, so ask ahead
examples: 주말이라 그 카페 사람 많을지도 몰라요. 예약하고 가요.
It's the weekend so that cafe might be packed — let's reserve.
Practical planning hedge
답장 늦을지도 몰라. 나 오늘 회의 빡세거든.
I might be slow to reply — I've got back-to-back meetings today.
빡세다 = grueling, casual; 거든 gives the reason
면접 결과 다음 주에 나올지도 몰라서 계속 메일 확인하고 있어요.
The interview result might come next week, so I keep checking my email.
면접 = job interview; job-hunt anxiety
mistakes: Don't use 모르다 to mean 'don't know' here — 올지도 몰라요 means 'might come,' not 'I don't know if it comes.'
For a past possibility use -았/었을지도 몰라요 (왔을지도 몰라요), not 올지도 몰랐어요 unless you mean a past frame of mind.

english: is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)
formNote: Attach -기 마련이다 directly to any verb or adjective stem with no sound change (늙다 → 늙기 마련이다, 바쁘다 → 바쁘기 마련이다, 실수하다 → 실수하기 마련이다). It states a general truth — something that inevitably happens by nature. A very common equivalent is -게 마련이다 (실수하게 마련이다), which means the same thing. It's used for life truths and proverb-like remarks.
usage: Everyone is bound to make mistakes
When you're busy you're bound to forget
Cheap things are bound to be low quality
examples: 혼자 살면 처음엔 외롭기 마련이에요. 곧 적응돼요.
Living alone, you're bound to feel lonely at first. You'll adjust soon.
Relatable to newcomers; 적응되다 = get used to it
연애 초반엔 다 콩깍지가 씌기 마련이지.
In the early days of dating, everyone's bound to be lovestruck.
콩깍지 씌다 = blinded by love; dating idiom
월급날 지나면 통장은 텅 비기 마련이에요.
After payday, your bank account is bound to end up empty.
통장 텅텅 = empty account; money humor for 20s-30s
mistakes: Don't use it for a one-time specific event ('I'm bound to be late today' is wrong) — it's for general, repeating truths.
Attach to the plain stem, not -는: it's 실수하기 마련이다 / 실수하게 마련이다, never 실수하는 마련이다.

english: no point doing it / whether you do it or not (the result's the same)
formNote: Attach -나 마나 to a vowel- or ㄹ-ending stem (보다 → 보나 마나) and -으나 마나 to a consonant-ending stem (먹다 → 먹으나 마나); ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ (살다 → 사나 마나). It literally pits 'whether you do (-나)' against 'whether you don't (마나, from 말다),' concluding it makes no difference. Very often it stands as a fixed adverb 보나 마나 = 'obviously / clearly.'
usage: That's a pointless thing to say
examples: 보나 마나 또 늦을 거야. 걔 원래 그래.
He'll obviously be late again. That's just how he is.
보나 마나 as 'obviously'; casual
세일 가나 마나예요. 인기 사이즈는 벌써 다 품절이거든요.
No point going to the sale — the popular sizes are already sold out.
품절 = sold out; shopping reality
걔한테 비밀 말하나 마나야. 어차피 다 소문나거든.
There's no point telling him a secret — it'll get out anyway.
소문나다 = become rumor; 어차피 = anyway
mistakes: 마나 comes from 말다, so don't write 마라/말아 here — the fixed shape is just -(으)나 마나.
It's verb-only; you can't say an adjective like 예쁘나 마나. Stick to action verbs.

english: half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)
formNote: Attach -는 둥 마는 둥 to a verb stem (먹다 → 먹는 둥 마는 둥, 듣다 → 듣는 둥 마는 둥); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (놀다 → 노는 둥 마는 둥). It pairs the verb with 말다 ('not do it') to paint an action done so half-heartedly it's barely done at all. It's usually followed by 하다 or another verb describing what you did instead, often with a distracted or rushed nuance.
usage: 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 했어요
I barely picked at my food
대답을 하는 둥 마는 둥 하더라고요
공부를 하는 둥 마는 둥 해
듣는 둥 마는 둥 하지 마
examples: 아침에 늦어서 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 하고 뛰어나왔어요.
I was late, so I barely touched my breakfast and ran out.
Hurried morning; very relatable
걔는 내 말을 듣는 둥 마는 둥 하고 계속 폰만 봤어.
He half-listened to me and just kept staring at his phone.
폰만 보다 = glued to phone; mild annoyance
주말 내내 일하는 둥 마는 둥 하면서 넷플릭스만 봤어요.
All weekend I sort of worked but mostly just watched Netflix.
Honest WFH confession; 내내 = the whole time
mistakes: Don't change 마는 to 말는 — the modifier of 말다 here is 마는 (the ㄹ drops before -는).
It always uses present -는 둥; don't say 먹은 둥 마는 둥 for the half-hearted meaning.

english: also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)
formNote: Attach -ㄹ 겸 to vowel-ending stems (보다 → 볼 겸) and -을 겸 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을 겸); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (놀다 → 놀 겸). 겸 means 'combining' two aims, so you do one action to serve two purposes at once. It very often comes in pairs: A-(으)ㄹ 겸 B-(으)ㄹ 겸 (= 'partly to A, partly to B'). After it usually comes the main action.
usage: I take a walk partly to get some air
I walk there, also to get some exercise
I'm going to Seoul, partly to see a friend
Let's meet, and grab a meal while we're at it
examples: 바람도 쐴 겸 머리도 식힐 겸 한강에 나왔어요.
I came out to the Han River partly for fresh air, partly to clear my head.
Paired 겸...겸; 머리 식히다 = clear one's head
맛집 탐방도 할 겸 데이트 겸 해서 성수동 갔어요.
We went to Seongsu-dong both to hit good restaurants and for a date.
성수동 = trendy Seoul area; 탐방 = exploring
운동도 할 겸 출근은 자전거로 해요.
I commute by bike, partly to get some exercise.
Practical lifestyle reason; 출근 = commute to work
mistakes: Don't use -는 겸 — it's the future modifier -(으)ㄹ + 겸 (볼 겸), not 보는 겸.
겸 needs a following main action; it can't end the sentence alone like a full verb (say 볼 겸 왔어요, not just 볼 겸이에요).

english: tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)
formNote: 편 means 'side/leaning,' so this softens a statement to 'rather' instead of 'very.' Verbs take -는 편이다 (먹다 → 먹는 편이다), adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 편이다 (크다 → 큰 편이다, 작다 → 작은 편이다). For past habits use -(으)ㄴ 편이었다. It's perfect for hedged self-description, so you sound modest rather than absolute.
usage: 저는 매운 거 잘 먹는 편이에요
I'm on the side of handling spicy food well
I'm a bit of a lightweight with alcohol
My salary is on the lower side
examples: 저는 집순이라서 주말엔 집에 있는 편이에요.
I'm a homebody, so I tend to stay in on weekends.
집순이 = stay-at-home type; popular self-label
여긴 다른 동네보다 월세가 싼 편이라 들어왔어요.
Rent here is on the cheaper side than other areas, so I moved in.
Comparing neighborhoods; housing talk
저는 낯을 좀 가리는 편이라 회식이 부담돼요.
I'm rather shy with new people, so company dinners stress me out.
낯을 가리다 = be shy with strangers; 부담되다 = feel pressured
mistakes: Match the modifier to word type: verbs use -는 편 (먹는 편), adjectives use -(으)ㄴ 편 (큰 편) — don't say 크는 편.
It means 'relatively,' so don't pair it with 아주/완전 ('totally'); that contradicts the softening nuance.

english: do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)
formNote: Attach -기는 하다 to a verb or adjective stem, repeating the verb's meaning in 하다 (먹다 → 먹기는 하다, 좋다 → 좋기는 하다). In speech 기는 almost always contracts to 긴 (먹긴 해요). It concedes one point while implying a 'but,' usually followed by 그런데/근데 or -지만. For other tenses, conjugate the final 하다: 먹기는 했어요 (I did eat, but...), 좋기는 할 거예요.
usage: I'll go, but I'll be late
I do know it, but I can't explain it
examples: 그 사람 착하긴 한데 좀 제 스타일은 아니에요.
He is nice, but he's just not my type.
Dating soft no; 착하다 = kind
회사 다니긴 다니는데 요즘 이직 생각 중이에요.
I am working at the company, but I'm thinking of switching jobs lately.
이직 = job change; honest career talk
맵긴 매운데 진짜 맛있어서 계속 손이 가요.
It is spicy, but it's so good I can't stop reaching for it.
손이 가다 = keep reaching for; food talk
mistakes: Don't drop the second verb's meaning — 가긴 하다 repeats the action; you can also fully repeat as 가긴 가다, but not just 가는 하다.
It sets up a contrast, so it sounds incomplete without the following 'but' clause; 좋긴 해요 alone hangs unless context implies the qualifier.
